summary:
Attention is all you need
Quoting @athleticKoder
She dumped me last night.
Not because I don't listen.
Not because I'm always on my phone.
Not even because I forgot our anniversary (twice).
But because,
in her exact words:
"You only pay attention to the parts of what I say that you think are important."
I stared at her for a moment and realized...
She just perfectly described the attention mechanism in transformers.
Turns out I wasn't being a bad boyfriend. I was being mathematically optimal.
See, in conversations (and transformers), you don't give equal weight to every word. Some words matter more for understanding context. Attention figures out exactly HOW important each word should be.
Here's the beautiful math:
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QK^T / √d_k)V
Breaking it down:
Q (Query): "What am I looking for?"
K (Key): "What info is available?"
V (Value): "What is that info?"
d_k: Key dimension (for scaling)
Think library analogy:
You have a question (Query). Books have titles (Keys) and content (Values). Attention finds which books are most relevant.
Step-by-step with "The cat sat on the mat":
Step 1: Create Q, K, VEach word → three vectors via learned matrices W_Q, W_K, W_V
For "cat":
Query: "What should I attend to when processing 'cat'?"
Key: "I am 'cat'"
Value: "Here's cat info"
Step 2: Calculate scoresQK^T = how much each word should attend to others
Processing "sat"? High similarity with "cat" (cats sit) and "mat" (where sitting happens).
Step 3: Scale by √d_kPrevents dot products from getting too large, keeps softmax balanced.
Step 4: SoftmaxConverts scores to probabilities:
"cat": 0.4 (subject)
"sat": 0.3 (action)
"mat": 0.2 (location)
"on": 0.1 (preposition)
"the": 0.1 (article)
Step 5: Weight valuesMultiply each word's value by attention weight, sum up. Now "sat" knows it's most related to "cat" and "mat".
Multi-Head Magic:Transformers do this multiple times in parallel:
Head 1: Subject-verb relationships
Head 2: Spatial ("on", "in", "under")
Head 3: Temporal ("before", "after")
Head 4: Semantic similarity
Each head learns different relationship types.
Why This Changed Everything:
Before: RNNs = reading with flashlight (one word at a time, forget the beginning)
After: Attention = floodlights on entire sentence with dimmer switches
This is why ChatGPT can:
Remember 50 messages ago
Know "it" refers to something specific
Understand "bank" = money vs river based on context
The Kicker:Models learn these patterns from data alone. Nobody programmed grammar rules. It figured out language structure just by predicting next words.
Attention is how AI learned to read between the lines.
Just like my therapist helped me understand my focus patterns, maybe understanding transformers helps us see how we decide what matters.
Now if only I could implement multi-head attention in dating... 🤖
Still waiting for "scaled dot-product listening" to be invented.

Quoting @NandoDF
The only bitter lesson is that LLMs have succeeded beyond any expert expectations.
Underpinning LLMs is the idea of scaling, which is too often misunderstood as more parameters. Scaling is about using massive compute effectively to maximise the throughput of data ingestion into the learning process to obtain more capable models.
We are still far from hitting the limits in this. We are still compute hungry because there is a ton more we could achieve if only we had more compute, from experimental ablations to data acquisition and curation.
Scaling is largely about data and evals. The models are now trained on almost all the web and equally large (but growing) self generated synthetic data. sifting through such vasts quantities of data (the whole of the human creation) requires formidable engineering and intelligent ideas. This is what differentiates most models.
AI is finally in the hands of billions of users, and with it come billions of tasks - every reasonable user need. This scaling in tasks and evaluations is many orders of magnitude larger than pre-LLMs.
Having the right architecture matters, but we know several alternatives could all work well, eg replacing attention in Transformers for RNNs and interleaving such layers with local layers. What matters is fine ablations to maximise hardware usage. This is the realm of sophisticated high-precision engineering. It encompasses semiconductor design, datacenter design, distributed systems, MFU, etc. There is fascinating work on flow matching, JEPA, sparser MoEs, etc, that is all consistent with scaling.
I’m terrible at predictions, but in this we have stayed the course. There’s been pleasant surprises like the effectiveness of reasoning, which while allowing for less parameters, still demands even more compute.
Sparser multimodal MoEs also will allow for better continual learning. This is an old idea, eg which is finally being done at scale.
Successful scaling is mostly about organising people into effective teams for research, development and production. They have to be teams of happy and ambitious people who put the team first. Yes, tech VCs and CEOs: work life balance matters to achieve prologued success, something I think @demishassabis did really well at @GoogleDeepMind and which I promote at @MicrosoftAI.
Bitter lesson: it really is all about scaling and hard work by thousands of amazing people. Hardly bitter, but hopeful and inspiring.

title: Yam Peleg (@Yampeleg)
summary:
Karpathy just dropped a code that:
1. Trains a tokenizer (rust).
2. Pretrains a GPT model on FineWeb.
3. SFT on chat data (smoltalk) & multiple choice questions & tool use.
4. RL (GRPO) on GSM8K.
5. Evaluates on ARC, MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval.
6. Run Inference with: KV cache, prefill/decode and tool-use (python sandbox).
Under 8K lines of code.
Quoting @karpathy
Excited to release new repo: nanochat!
(it's among the most unhinged I've written).
Unlike my earlier similar repo nanoGPT which only covered pretraining, nanochat is a minimal, from scratch, full-stack training/inference pipeline of a simple ChatGPT clone in a single, dependency-minimal codebase. You boot up a cloud GPU box, run a single script and in as little as 4 hours later you can talk to your own LLM in a ChatGPT-like web UI.
It weighs ~8,000 lines of imo quite clean code to:
- Train the tokenizer using a new Rust implementation
- Pretrain a Transformer LLM on FineWeb, evaluate CORE score across a number of metrics
- Midtrain on user-assistant conversations from SmolTalk, multiple choice questions, tool use.
- SFT, evaluate the chat model on world knowledge multiple choice (ARC-E/C, MMLU), math (GSM8K), code (HumanEval)
- RL the model optionally on GSM8K with "GRPO"
- Efficient inference the model in an Engine with KV cache, simple prefill/decode, tool use (Python interpreter in a lightweight sandbox), talk to it over CLI or ChatGPT-like WebUI.
- Write a single markdown report card, summarizing and gamifying the whole thing.
Even for as low as ~$100 in cost (~4 hours on an 8XH100 node), you can train a little ChatGPT clone that you can kind of talk to, and which can write stories/poems, answer simple questions. About ~12 hours surpasses GPT-2 CORE metric. As you further scale up towards ~$1000 (~41.6 hours of training), it quickly becomes a lot more coherent and can solve simple math/code problems and take multiple choice tests. E.g. a depth 30 model trained for 24 hours (this is about equal to FLOPs of GPT-3 Small 125M and 1/1000th of GPT-3) gets into 40s on MMLU and 70s on ARC-Easy, 20s on GSM8K, etc.
My goal is to get the full "strong baseline" stack into one cohesive, minimal, readable, hackable, maximally forkable repo. nanochat will be the capstone project of LLM101n (which is still being developed). I think it also has potential to grow into a research harness, or a benchmark, similar to nanoGPT before it. It is by no means finished, tuned or optimized (actually I think there's likely quite a bit of low-hanging fruit), but I think it's at a place where the overall skeleton is ok enough that it can go up on GitHub where all the parts of it can be improved.
Link to repo and a detailed walkthrough of the nanochat speedrun is in the reply.

title: Yam Peleg (@Yampeleg)
summary:
CLI Agents | Week 1 Field Report
Claude Code vs Codex-max vs Gemini 3
I used all three as my main daily drivers this week for coding, research, sysadmin, automation..
Here are my personal opinions from real world usage:
---
Claude Code:
- Still has the BEST CLI. Hands down. Packed with a ton of unique killer features.
- I use it as my daily driver, even when not doing code. Best for everything *around* code: general computer use, browsing, research, brainstorming, pair programming human-in-the-loop, etc.
- The Subagents + Custom MCP + Custom Commands are real killer features.
- Skills are a bit unpredictable in my opinion. I tend not to use them.
- Subagents are A KILLER FEATURE. Not specifically the ones you customize (they are nice), but the ability to delegate to a sub-agent predictably just by asking Claude to use them, even in parallel: INSANE. I use it all the time.
- Agent SDK:
I gave the agent sdk shit at the beginning.
I was wrong. It’s fire.
I use it all the time.
I have MCPs that use it; all agents get access to the MCPs and they call Claude Code.
- Daily driver: I use it for everything I do.
Seriously everything.
- Note: It’s also strong for coding.
Claude is a great coder. No one is denying it.
But there are better alternatives today (as of this moment) for pure code.
Claude is a great coder but also gets easily distracted therefore it won’t go on working on the same task for hours on its own.
Overall: Daily Driver.
(for pure coding: continue reading)
---
Codex & GPT-5.1-Codex-Max
- For heavy pure coding & big refactors.
- It will grind through ANYTHING mostly on its own.
- Also incredible for research. I saw it powering through an open research question, going on its own to read papers, download them as PDFs, then converting them to txt and reading them.
- It can be weirdly unconfident sometimes and needs encouragement.
- Not the best option for tight human-in-the-loop iterative work, explanation below.
- Forget about sysadmin tasks, codex doesn't like them, when you insist to do something in a certine way, codex would do it at the end (it definitly can!! it just "doesn't like it") but on the next time this situation happen, it would not.
Example: connecting to remote machines, etc.
It definitly can do it, but it seems like it "doesn't like it".
(If it makes sense)
- Tool calling and MCP: These are there but in a very limited way, these are not running as smooth as Claude Code's CLI.
Iv'e seen many times codex trying to use an MCP, it crashes/times-out/random-bug in its face, so codex just moves and do the same thing via bash.
- No need for sub-agents because Codex will just bruteforce anything on its own.
Again: perfect for "send and forget", less for iterative human-in-the-loop.
Overall: Best coder. Fire and forget.
(and it doesn’t really want you to be involved while working)
----
Gemini CLI + Gemini-3:
- THE BEST web search. Integrated Google Search is unmatched. period.
(and this is incredibly important for research)
- Coding: In theory it’s insane for coding. (and it is).
But it also has a tendency to just rewrite your files from scratch and redesign your entire app.
Don’t get me wrong: it’s a beast for coding.
But it can be uneasy to control or work with iteratively human-in-the-loop-style when editing files.
It will eventually do things "your way" if you ask it enough but this requires a little bit of convincing.
- Computer use: It is incredible for controling a linux machine and linux sysadmin.
General computer use works very well!
It understands the system on a deeper level than the other models and can tweak very heavy internal things in linux.
- Reverse Engineering on it's own:
(this is not a joke)
This model is an absolute monster.
If you send it to "kill" a target, this target is DEAD.
I have seen it starting to reverse engineer compiled binary files on my machine to understand how to configure them.
Gemini models were always good for RE but I have never seen a model doing it unprompted.
Seriously impressed.
- Insane context length:
It has an insanly long context length.
And it is not afraid to use it.
You tell it to read EVERY file in a folder.
It will read EVERY FILE in that folder.
It even has a tool for it "ReadManyFiles".
(why was it commented out? I commented it back in lol)
- Rate Limits: At the moment, its heavily rate-limited.
In real day-to-day work I personally burn all my quota in ~1 hour.
- About the CLI engine: It’s heavier than Claude Code, custom scroll handling interferes with power-user tools like tmux. In my pesonal opinion i would have loved more flexibility so I could integrate it better with the tools I currently use.
Overall: BEAST.
(just be careful with it)

I released something that has been useful to me over the last few months:
Basically it's a tool that spiders docs into a single md file and then I tell Composer to make a "grep index" of the file. The models are good at doing it.
I have a bunch of the docs I care about in docs/external so you can see what it looks like, like mdn-css, javascript, typescript, anthropic, langgraph, react, etc.
Have composer do a few passes with the prompt "check this and make sure it's accurate, comprehensive and thorough" and you end up with a very well indexed file quickly.
With local docs like this you can have a coding model refer to those docs and it grounds their code much better.
It seems to work better than built-in Indexing in Cursor, which is a black box. With grep indexing you can test the results yourself and it is easy to read. Since the models are so good at using grep now, it works as well or better than semantic search.
The spidering tool is pretty simple and not for production. It's meant to just spider docs you care about on a project.
For the docs aggregator tool, I had Composer write and test the "changes in docs re-spider functionality" this afternoon but honestly did not check it that closely. Use at your own peril. May or may not work.

Thoughts after a few days with Opus as daily driver:
Anthropic srsly cooked with Opus.
Is it "the best" at "everything"?
No. It’s not THE BEST for every single task I had in my normal daily work.
For a huge chunk of work it absolutely feels like it though.
I still use Codex-Max and Gemini-3 as well.
Each of the 3 leading models is great for different tasks.
Notably, for:
1. Internet access: Gemini CLI with its GoogleSearch tool is still unmatched.
(For all other agents I use Perplexity via MCP; it beats all the built-in search.)
2. Academic research: Codex is unmatched.
Apart from these use cases, all 3 models are very close it terms of usefulness.
But also very different in their capabilities.
It’s hard to describe which model would be better for what, but all 3 have different tasks they are better at than the others.
You sort of "get a feeling" at some point for which model to use for what.
BUT
(hear me out)
The crazy thing about Opus-4.5 is not Opus.
Is how well it works with it's harness.
Yes. Claude Code.
Claude Code as a CLI agent is on a different league:
Full machine control, browser, configs, sub-agents, tinkering, send-and-forget.
Even when it was Sonnet-only and clearly weaker than GPT-5-Codex, the harness was already irreplaceable.
I used to run my own forked “agent” for months because I needed customization.
Now I simply don’t need it. Claude Code is customizable enough, and when combining it with Agent SDK you can just do anything you ever want.
I stopped caring Claude Code is not open source. I can just shape it however I want now without touching its code.
(Yes, there are still dumb bugs in CC, e.g. using many sub agents in parallel will nuke your machine even with 256GB RAM.)
But overall, Claude Code is a powerhouse.
Nothing gets close.
---
How I code with agents:
For hard problems I work on daily basis, I am still much better (and also much faster) than current gen LLMs.
These tasks I just myself, usually without trying to delegate anything.
When the code takes shape, I usually start delegating small (isolated) parts of the code but heavily supervise and edit for quality.
For everything below, I try to delegate as much as possible to the agents.
AI coding style got much better in 2025, so some of the code I get don't even need any editing.
(disposible code for single use hacks & tricks i don't even try looking into)
All planning & designing & architecture I do myself.
Full stop.
Coding delegations are usually incredibly well defined and "micro-managed" without giving the full picture.
I am def not "vibe-coding" with Agents but I do use LLMs on daily basis now and didn't do so a year ago.
---
Head-to-head, Opus vs Codex vs Gemini:
It is close.
As standalone models they are all insane.
We didn't have this level of models two weeks ago.
But overall, Opus + Claude Code is on another level.
Everything else feels like a coding tool, a very powerful tool, but still just a tool for coding.
But Claude Code (especially with Opus) is a full computer-use agent.
(which also happens to be the best-ish for most coding tasks)

summary:
My problem with Claude Skills is that they are not skills.
Nothing forces Claude to actually use them.
Claude does whatever it wants.
Even if you specify it explicitly, it's not guaranteed.
These are not skills.
These are just md files.
They can be useful, like manuals or tutorials.
But for some reason, the only thing ppl use them for is:
"You are a professional software engineer"
"You run tests after making changes"
"You think step by step"
Do you really think a model trained on the entire internet doesn't know to run tests?!
This is nearly the only thing you can find when you look inside the actual "skills" published online.
Every GitHub repo, every tutorial, every example.
Even the official examples from the actual creators.
(although they are a bit better than github)
You guys seriously think this would work?
The ONLY way prompts can be valuable is including NEW information.
Things the model DOESN'T know.
Things you CAN-NOT find on the internet.
For example:
- Information about YOUR project.
- Workflow YOU use when working on YOUR project.
- Results YOU found through experiments.
- Experience YOU gained over time.
- Commands YOU use every day.
- YOUR Passwords. YOUR Credentials. YOUR Internal documentation.
- Workflows that only sense for YOUR specific case.
Not BS like:
- Style guides that are general: "how to write good code"
- Personas.
- Step-by-step debugging philosophies.
If you, a flesh and blood human, came to work with me
And on the first day I tell you:
"make sure you run tests every time"
You would say:
"k cool. now what?"
But if I handed you a manual with actual examples of things I use every day BY MYSELF?
- Maybe the actual API of our internal software..
- Maybe a cmd line cheatsheet from my bash history..
- Maybe passwords, path locations, credentials..
- Processes WE actually go through.
- The way WE do CI in OUR project.
Would it help you?
More than "run tests every time"?
Yes, because it is practical.
- You can follow it.
- You can mimic it.
- You can use it.
You don't really need me to tell you stupid basic shit like
"break apart your problem into smaller parts"
Yes, for sure, do it.
But everyone knows this already.
Bro, just take my fucking real bash history.
Do as I do.
Faster and easier for everyone.
Not because I am some sort of a bash god
(i am, but thats a different story)
Because you can't Google this.
It only makes sense FOR OUR PROJECT.
---
This is what I actually use for Claude Code:
- One file concatenated always to the system prompt.
- Inside of it: references to tutorials saved as md files.
- All in a single folder.
- And a small instruction telling the model to use the same folder to save more tutorials if it discovers a new thing that could be useful.
That's all.
And it actually works, this folder keeps growing and opus reads files from it all the time.
collected tutorials about connecting to my own remote machines, actual domains, actual keys, actual paths, actual workflows, actual useful commands to use..
Everything is unique to my setup, my projects.
If I gave them to you and we work together, you would also benefit.
That is the point.
---
What about processes?
Good that you asked.
You want Claude to run tests every time it edits a code?
Make it fucking automatic.
Why do you even let claude decide about this?
Force it to react to something outside its control.
Not make decisions by itself.
These things are probabilistic.
NOTHING will it follow instructions 100% of the times.
---
I seriously went through a ton of "skills" online, trying to find useful ones I could use by myself.
Nothing.
It's all AI slop.
Pasting it back into the model makes no sense.
The only real one I saw was from HuggingFace.
Go check it out, they wrote a full tutorial in it.
With actual commands, code, examples... etc..
This is why it works.
Just tell the model what you would tell another human.
It would not be "you are a software engineer"
For a very good reason.

title: Yam Peleg (@Yampeleg)
summary:
For anyone curious how I manage hundreds of agents via WhatsApp:
I just reply to them.
My system automatically routes my msg to the specific agent that sent the msg.
They all live on the same machine.
Spawning each other autonomously, on default they report to their parent agent.
I am DMing only with "Commander Claude"
(srsly it's already overwhelming enough..)
However, all agents also have a tool to send me direct msgs.
They nearly never do this, they usually just reporting up the chain of command.
All sub-agent msgs get to a single WhatsApp group.
If I reply to a msg directly it goes automatically to the sending agent.
If I just send a msg to the group, it spawns a new agent with it as a prompt.
(and a system prompt explaining all of this)
I just wanted to run some jobs in parallel with this.
But they all multiply and delegate all the time, I just found myself going walkie-talkie:
*click*
"somebody find me the agent that was working on ___"
* walkie-talkie radio static sound *
And I get a msg back from that agent.
(after the new one I spawned found him, woke him up with its context, prompted him to contact me).
"All agents be advised, the knowledge base was updated with documentation of ___"
And then I see on my own terminal, out of nowhere, in the input of the Claude Code that I am using, somebody is typing:
"BROADCAST FROM COMMANDER PELEG: Check the knowledge base ({path I didn't even mention but the new agent found it and went out of its way to help other agents})"
Voice notes are transcribed automatically so I literally just talk into my phone like a walkie-talkie, walking around, driving, whatever.
The agent hears me, delegate, multiply, however they want, then execute.
The agents build tools and register them in a shared file so the next agent that spawns already knows what's available and can use them.
I sent a voice msg today about making some docs for all these tools they built for themselves.
Then ended up with 86 parallel Opus calls in different tmux sessions generating documents from 3000 conversations transcripts I didn’t even know about lol.
I didn't orchestrate any of this lol.
They all figured it out and delegated on their own.
The whole thing runs all the time, I just talk to them via voice and they do their own thing in the background.
Everything running with dangerously bypass permissions, yolo, no sandboxs.. nothing ever happens lol
(stuff do happen from time to time but it’s all backed up and i like speed so yolo)
This is not any product or an open source project btw, srsly it’s insanely simple you can vibe code your own in 5 mins.
It's just an ugly hacky script with ~400 lines.
Held together by “opus ma man, there is another bug in the server”.
But it works and I'm productive as hell with this, who would have thought.
My primary IDE is now WhatsApp lamo

title: Yam Peleg (@Yampeleg)
summary:
Excited to share PostTrainBench: a benchmark for a question that feels increasingly important for AI R&D automation: can frontier CLI agents autonomously post-train LLMs?
In PostTrainBench, we give an agent a base model, a target benchmark, one H100, and 10 hours, then let it handle the rest of the workflow, including finding data, writing training code, debugging, iterating, and submitting a final model. We provide no starter pipeline and no predefined strategy.
Current agents do surprisingly decently, but there’s still a large gap to instruct models trained by humans. The best agent reaches 23.2% weighted average vs 51.1% for official instruct baselines (but this isn't exactly apples to apples, since official post-training usually exceeds the 10h / 1-GPU budget).
At the same time, agents can already be surprisingly strong in targeted settings. GPT-5.1 Codex Max gets Gemma-3-4B to 89% on BFCL vs 67% for the official instruct model.
We also found some reward hacking. Agents sometimes trained on test data, swapped in existing instruction-tuned checkpoints, or used unauthorized API keys for synthetic data generation.
PostTrainBench is useful both for tracking progress in automated AI research and for studying the failure modes and sandboxing problems that come with it.
collaborated with @full__rank @hrdkbhatnagar @AmyPrb @karinanguyen @MatthiasBethge @maksym_andr

title: Yam Peleg (@Yampeleg)
summary:
Scale Is All You Need.
Quoting @bojie_li
Closed labs hide model sizes. They can't hide what their models know, and what a model knows is an indicator on how big it is.
Reasoning compresses. Factual knowledge doesn't. So you can size a frontier model from black-box API calls alone, and across releases you can literally watch a single fact arrive in the parameters over time.
For three years, my friends Jiyan He and Zihan Zheng have been asking frontier LLMs the same question: "what do you know about USTC Hackergame?", a CTF contest. May 2024: GPT-4o invented fake titles. Feb 2025: Claude 3.7 Sonnet listed 19 verified 2023 challenges. By April 2026, frontier models recall specific challenges across consecutive years.
After DeepSeek-V4 dropped, I instructed my agent to spend four days autonomously turning that habit into Incompressible Knowledge Probes (IKP) — 1,400 questions, 7 tiers of obscurity, 188 models, 27 vendors. Three findings:
1/ You can approximately size any black-box LLM from factual accuracy alone. Penalized accuracy is log-linear in log(params), R² = 0.917 on 89 open-weight models from 135M to 1.6T params. Project closed APIs onto the curve → GPT-5.5 ~9T, Claude Opus 4.7 ~4T, GPT-5.4 ~2.2T, Claude Sonnet 4.6 ~1.7T, Gemini 2.5 Pro ~1.2T (90% CI: 0.3-3x size).
2/ Citation count and h-index don't predict whether a frontier model recognizes a researcher. Two researchers with similar citation profiles get very different responses. Models memorize impact — work that shaped a field, not many incremental papers.
3/ Factual capacity doesn't compress over time. Across 96 open-weight models across 3 years, the IKP time coefficient is statistically zero, rejecting the Densing-Law prediction of +0.0117/month at p<10⁻¹⁵. Reasoning benchmarks saturate; factual capacity keeps scaling with parameters.

Today we release Token Superposition Training (TST), a modification to the standard LLM pretraining loop that produces a 2-3× wall-clock speedup at matched FLOPs without changing the model architecture, optimizer, tokenizer, or training data.
During the first third of training, the model reads and predicts contiguous bags of tokens, averaging their embeddings on the input side and predicting the next bag with a modified cross-entropy on the output side. For the remainder of the run, it trains normally on next-token prediction. The inference-time model is identical to one produced by conventional pretraining.
Validated at 270M, 600M, and 3B dense scales, and at 10B-A1B MoE.
The work on TST was led by @bloc97_, @gigant_theo, and @theemozilla.

Not your harness, not your time.
Quoting @DimitrisPapail
Found something in my daily use of Claude Code that validates our Memento results:
Claude Code flushes the KV cache after some idle period, and when I come back past that the model is noticeably harder to work with.
Conjecture: post-flush, the model is no longer continuing its trajectory. It's shoved into a weird OOD regime where it has to simulate what has happened from the tokens and resume from a reconstruction.
Which is much harder than just continuing!!
We measured this effect in our paper. KV states (soft embeddings) carry information that text tokens don't, even when attention is masked.
Bottom line: If you flush your cache you lose a lot of accuracy!

Quoting @Badtheorylabs
Today we are Introducing BTL-3.
A 27B open-weight agent model built for agentic coding, structural tool use . The complete thing fits in one 8.39GB file under 2.5 bits per parameter smaller than an 8B model in fp16, and retains 92.2% of the 27B itelligence
BTL-3 is trained for the loop real agents live in: reason, act, inspect the result, recover, continue. It handles single, sequential, and parallel tool calls and knows when the right move is no tool call at all.
HumanEval: 95.12% pass@1
BFCL v4 AST: 88.5% (full 1,240-case set)
Multiple tool calls: 95.5%
Tool-call abstention: 91.2%
262K context architecture
Two editions, both open today.
BTL-3 is the maximum-quality checkpoint, for Transformers and vLLM.
BTL-3 Compact is the entire model in one standalone 8.39GB GGUF. No base download. No reconstruction. One file, one command, a running agent.
Compressing 27B this far normally destroys a model. Standard quantization couldn't do it, so we built the stack ourselves: packed AVQ2 decoder tensors, affine INT4, measured precision islands, packed vocabulary matrices, rank-32 output correction, behavioral repair. 2,416 tensors byte-verified at export.
Then we tested whether the agent survived. On a fresh sealed 100-turn tool-contract gate, Compact retained 92.2% of teacher-correct behavior 100% on single, parallel, sequential, and abstention calls.
43 tok/s generation on an RTX PRO 6000. Fully local. Nothing leaves your machine.

Ok wow. BTL-3 is a 27-billion-parameter open-weight agent model designed for agentic coding, structural tool use, and reasoning. It fits in a single 8.39GB file, retains 92.2% of the original intelligence, and handles reasoning, acting, inspecting results, recovering, and continuing across single, sequential, and parallel tool calls.

The model achieves high performance on benchmarks like HumanEval with 95.12% pass@1 and demonstrates robust multi-tool call capabilities. There is also a compact version, BTL-3 Compact, which is a fully standalone 8.39GB GGUF file, fully local, with no need for reconstruction or base downloads. It maintains 92.2% of the teacher model's behavior after aggressive compression involving AVQ2, INT4 quantization, and other techniques, verified across 2,416 tensors.

Both versions are open source, available on Hugging Face and GitHub, and run at 43 tokens per second on an RTX PRO 6000. The models are released under Apache-2.0 and MIT licenses, respectively, aiming to democratize AI through open science and open source.
